title: From Chmielnik to Israel: Aliyah and the Landsleit Network
summary: The early departures and later support networks reveal how Chmielnik’s people carried communal ties into new lives abroad.

![Chmielnik, the town the emigrants left behind](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg/1920px-Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A departure remembered by name

The Chmielnik memorial book remembers emigration not as a statistic but as a list of neighbors who left. Its account begins, “In the years 1919–1920, they made aliyah from Chmielnik,” and names [Avraham Vigodny](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_ea8e17a83e1bf3d7034484fc), [Mendel Rosenzweig](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_3dea08ef7f31c63fdd4d804a), [Binyamin Eliezer Shamchugi (Friedman)](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_5b7ab40bb21abe3ef1b1ebc6), his wife [Deborah Abramovitz](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_0f35115839234d007689c02b), and [Yitzhak Ben-Tov (Grenk)](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_91a3bc622bf7bb04037a147b). These are the names preserved in the passage; the list should not be mistaken for a complete passenger roll or a record of everyone who left.

A separate passage says that the first group of Chmielnikers arrived in the Land of Israel on August 9, 1920. It names [Judah Arnreich](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_1069df817aa63ac92040d4a9) and [Motel Rosenblum](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_0996c1492a7bfc5d2209fe3a) among the first arrivals, and specifically calls Rosenblum one of the first two. The book does not make clear whether these two belonged to the group listed for 1919–1920, or whether that list and the “first group” passage describe overlapping but differently remembered departures. The safest account preserves both: a list of emigrants across those years, and a distinct recollection of an arrival on a precise day.

The book also records [later emigration](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_8e3851ad760b34f383963963), naming [Efraim Poper](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_c847ad861d2f258e21e47923) among those who left in subsequent years, before the war began in 1939. That later movement is a reminder that Chmielnik’s connection with Palestine and Israel was not a single exodus. It unfolded over time, through individual decisions and family journeys whose circumstances the surviving summary does not specify.

## A town in a changing Poland

The years 1919–1920 came just after the First World War, amid the reconstruction of Poland and upheaval across eastern Europe. Chmielnik, now in the Świętokrzyskie region, had become part of independent Poland after a period of partition and wartime occupation. That political transition supplies context, not an explanation for any named person’s choice: the memorial book does not say why Avraham Vigodny, the Rosenzweigs, the Shamchugis, or Ben-Tov left.

The wider record helps establish the scale of the community they departed. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos describes Chmielnik on the eve of the Second World War as a town of about 6,000 Jews, roughly four-fifths of its population. It notes livelihoods in craft and trade, Zionist and other political activity, and aid supported by American landsleit. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406&utm_source=openai)) Those facts illuminate the later network’s social setting, but they do not independently verify the book’s 1920 arrival date or the biographies of the emigrants.

The memorial book’s heading identifies a group of Chmielnik natives who settled in [Petah Tikva](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_7696eaf9757d7003c68ca1af), with others arriving later. It does not identify every settler or give a full chronology. Petah Tikva’s appearance matters because it shows the remembered destination was not only a broad national idea—“Israel”—but also a particular place where people from the same hometown could gather, work, and build new lives. The available evidence does not establish that all of the first arrivals settled there.

## From migration to mutual support

The memorial book’s account extends beyond the pioneers themselves. It remembers Chmielnikers in Israel meeting each year on 25 Tishrei to commemorate their destroyed hometown. Another passage describes an annual memorial ceremony for the town’s martyrs. These are records of organized remembrance: a community maintained ties not merely through shared origin, but through recurring dates, gatherings, and acts of commemoration.

In Israel, [Mordechai Zanshayn](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_8d8105ab3bab72954df37652) is identified as chairman of the Organization of Chmielnik Natives. [Moses Ben-Shahar](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_176fab7a01001cc7527acbf9) participated in negotiations over a site for the proposed [Beit Chmielnik](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_ff2501307e0a0593f1f2e730), a memorial project in Tel Aviv. The book records the proposal and the negotiations; it does not, in the evidence supplied here, establish that the planned building was completed. Its significance lies in the ambition it expresses: to give the dispersed landsleit a shared address for memory and communal life.

Across the Atlantic, [Moshe Leizer Mintz](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_fc039ef98d4b7c8d03c16024) appears as president of the Chmielnik Aid Committee in the United States. The memorial book places Israeli commemoration and American mutual aid within the same wider story of hometown organization. But it does not provide a ledger of assistance or explain how aid moved between overseas committees, individuals, and relatives still in Poland. Those details remain questions for further research into the association’s records and the lives of its members.

## The limits and legacy of the record

A Yizkor book preserves the community’s own memory, shaped by those who survived, emigrated, and later organized to remember. Its lists are invaluable precisely because they restore names. They are not, by themselves, complete migration records. The brief entries do not tell us whether named people traveled together, what route they took, who remained in Chmielnik, or what became of each family. Even where a relationship is explicit—Binyamin Eliezer Shamchugi and his wife Deborah Abramovitz—the account does not trace their subsequent lives.

Independent sources consulted add context about Chmielnik’s prewar population, work, and political and charitable institutions, but they do not independently confirm the specific emigrant names or August 9, 1920 arrival. The town’s later fate gives the landsleit’s work a particular weight: Yad Vashem documents the wartime ghetto and the destruction that followed. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406&utm_source=openai)) The annual gatherings and proposed Beit Chmielnik were not simply nostalgia. They were ways of sustaining relationships to a community that could no longer gather in its old home.

The story that survives is therefore both a migration story and a record of institution-building. The first departures carried Chmielnikers to new lives; later, associations in Israel and the United States helped turn shared origin into practical aid and durable remembrance. The next questions are personal as much as institutional: what became of the [Shamchugi-Friedman family](research:Binyamin Shamchugi and Deborah Abramovitz after their aliyah), and what records might trace the journeys and descendants of the early emigrants?
